title: Sex Linkage, Dosage Compensation and Non-Mendelian Inheritance

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Why does it matter which fly parent carries a recessive white-eye allele on the X, when it never mattered which Mendelian pea plant was the mother?
cards.back: Males and females carry different numbers of X chromosomes, so an X-linked allele reaches sons and daughters differently depending on the parent. An autosomal allele, without imprinting, gives the same F1 either way.
cards.quote: With the same parental genotypes, an ordinary non-imprinted autosomal allele gives the same F1 both ways.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: A male fly is {{c1::hemizygous}} for X-linked genes: one allele rather than a pair, so whatever his X carries is what shows.
cards.quote: A male is therefore hemizygous for white: one allele rather than a pair, so whatever his X carries is what you see.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: A white-eyed male fly is crossed to red-eyed females, and all offspring of both sexes are red-eyed. What does this show about the white allele?
cards.back: White is recessive: it shows only when no dominant allele is present.
cards.quote: the white-eyed male crossed to red-eyed females gave red-eyed offspring of both sexes, so white is recessive: it shows only when no dominant allele is present.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: In Drosophila, on which chromosome does the white gene sit, and what does the Y carry for it?
cards.back: The white gene sits on the X. The Y carries no copy.
cards.quote: The white gene sits on the X; the Y carries no copy.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: In Drosophila, a red-eyed X+X+ female is crossed to a white-eyed XwY male. What are the genotypes and eye colours of the F1 daughters and sons?
cards.back: Daughters are X+Xw and red-eyed; sons are X+Y and red-eyed. Each son gets his only X from his mother, so he is red-eyed; each daughter gets X+ from her mother and Xw from her father, and X+ is dominant.
cards.quote: Write X+ for red and Xw for white.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: In Drosophila, a white-eyed XwXw mother and a red-eyed X+Y father have offspring. Give each sex's eye colour and name the inheritance pattern.
cards.back: Daughters are red-eyed X+Xw; sons are white-eyed XwY. This is criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter, mother to son.
cards.quote: It shows criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter, mother to son.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: In Drosophila, the F1 from a red X+X+ female by white XwY male are intercrossed (X+Xw female by X+Y male). What F2 phenotypes by sex do you expect?
cards.back: All daughters are red (half X+X+, half X+Xw). Half the sons are white (XwY). Overall three red to one white, every white fly male.
cards.quote: The F2 expectation is three red to one white, every white fly male.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: From the intercross X+Xw female by X+Y male in Drosophila, 800 F2 flies are scored. Assuming ordinary segregation and half of each sex, how many white-eyed flies do you expect, and what fraction of the males are white?
cards.back: Males are half of 800, so 400; half of them are XwY, so 200 white flies, all male. White is 200/800 = 1/4 of all flies and 1/2 of the males. No females are white.
cards.why: Daughters always receive X+ from their father.
cards.quote: Sons get X+ or Xw from their mother, so half are white.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: A Drosophila cross gives all red-eyed daughters and all white-eyed sons. White is recessive and X-linked. What are the parents' genotypes?
cards.back: Mother XwXw (white) and father X+Y (red). Sons get only the mother's Xw and so are white; daughters get the father's X+ and the mother's Xw, so they are red.
cards.quote: It shows criss-cross inheritance: father to daughter, mother to son.
cards.section: One white-eyed male: follow the X

cards.front: Bridges crossed white XwXw females to red X+Y males. What exceptional offspring appeared, and how often?
cards.back: Roughly 1 in 1,600 offspring were exceptional: white daughters or red sons, instead of the expected red daughters and white sons.
cards.quote: Roughly 1 in 1,600 offspring were exceptional white daughters or red sons.
cards.section: The exceptions that tested the model

cards.front: Keeping white on the X, explain how a maternal meiotic error could produce an exceptional white daughter and an exceptional red son in Bridges' cross. What chromosome sets do they carry?
cards.back: Maternal nondisjunction gives eggs with XwXw or no X. XwXw egg plus Y sperm gives an XwXwY white daughter. An egg with no X plus X+ sperm gives an X+O red son.
cards.why: Rule: the white allele travels with the X chromosome.
cards.quote: XwXw egg plus Y sperm gives an XwXwY white daughter, with both X chromosomes from her mother.
cards.section: The exceptions that tested the model

cards.front: Why is an exceptional X+O red-eyed male fly expected to be sterile?
cards.back: His only X came from his father and he has no Y. In flies the Y is needed for male fertility.
cards.quote: His only X came from his father, and without a Y he should be sterile.
cards.section: The exceptions that tested the model

cards.front: What did matching Bridges' unusual eye-colour flies to unusual chromosome sets show about the white gene, and about sex determination in flies?
cards.back: It tied white to the X chromosome. It also showed that an XO fly is male and an XXY fly female, so the Y does not decide sex in flies.
cards.quote: Matching an unusual phenotype to an unusual chromosome set tied white to the X.
cards.section: The exceptions that tested the model

cards.front: Name two human metabolic enzyme deficiencies that are X-linked and much more common in males.
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and HPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome).
cards.quote: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (pentose phosphate pathway) and HPRT deficiency in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (nucleotide metabolism) are both much more common in males.
cards.section: The exceptions that tested the model

cards.front: Compare how XO and XXY individuals develop in humans and in Drosophila. What different rules explain the pattern?
cards.back: Humans: XO is female (Turner), XXY is male (Klinefelter), because a Y carrying SRY starts testis development. Flies: XO is male, XXY is female, because in a diploid fly X dose ordinarily sets sex and the Y is needed only for male fertility.
cards.why: Mammals read the Y; flies read X dose.
cards.quote: Thus XO individuals with Turner syndrome develop as females, while XXY individuals with Klinefelter syndrome develop as males.
cards.section: How sex is decided: mammal versus fly

cards.front: In most mammals, which gene on the Y chromosome starts testis development?
cards.back: SRY in humans, Sry in mice.
cards.quote: In most mammals, including mice and humans, one Y carrying SRY in humans or Sry in mice starts testis development.
cards.section: How sex is decided: mammal versus fly

cards.front: What experiment showed that Sry is sufficient for male development in mice?
cards.back: A 14-kilobase fragment containing Sry was added to chromosomally female (XX) mouse embryos; they developed testes.
cards.quote: In 1991 Koopman and colleagues added a 14-kilobase fragment containing Sry to chromosomally female mouse embryos; it was sufficient to make them develop testes.
cards.section: How sex is decided: mammal versus fly

cards.front: What signal sets female development in diploid Drosophila, and what gene does it switch on?
cards.back: High X dose (two X chromosomes) switches on Sex-lethal. It maintains its own activity through RNA splicing and steers splicing of genes below it.
cards.quote: Either way, high X dose switches on Sex-lethal in females, which maintains its own activity through RNA splicing and steers splicing of genes below it.
cards.section: How sex is decided: mammal versus fly

cards.front: In a simplified model with every X-linked copy fully active, an XX animal begins with {{c1::twice}} the X-linked dose of an XY or XO animal.
cards.quote: In a simplified model with every X-linked copy fully active, an XX animal begins with twice the dose of an XY or XO animal.

cards.front: What three strategies could equalise X-linked output between XX and XY animals, and which animals use them (mammals, flies, C. elegans)?
cards.back: Turn one of two X chromosomes down (mammals inactivate one female X), turn the single X up (flies, male X), or reduce output from both (C. elegans XX hermaphrodites).
cards.quote: Turn one of two X chromosomes down, turn the single X up, or reduce output from both.

cards.front: State Lyon's hypothesis for X inactivation in a female mouse.
cards.back: Each cell inactivates either its maternal or paternal X early in development, and its descendants keep that choice.
cards.quote: Mary Lyon proposed in 1961 that each cell of a female mouse inactivates either its maternal or paternal X early in development, and its descendants keep that choice.

cards.front: A female mammal is heterozygous for an X-linked allele. What does her tissue look like, and why do neighbouring cells match each other?
cards.back: She is a mosaic: patches of cell lineages expressing different X-linked alleles. A cell inactivates one X early on and its descendants keep that choice, so each patch is a clone.
cards.quote: A heterozygous female is therefore a mosaic, a patchwork of cell lineages expressing different X-linked alleles.

cards.front: In placental mammals the inactive X forms the condensed Barr body and is coated by {{c1::Xist}}, an RNA that appears not to encode protein.
cards.quote: In placental mammals the inactive X forms the condensed Barr body and is coated by Xist, an RNA that appears not to encode protein.

cards.front: What does it mean that Xist acts in cis, and what did mouse deletions show about it?
cards.back: It silences the chromosome that makes it. Deletions showed Xist is required for inactivation.
cards.quote: It acts in cis, silencing the chromosome that makes it.

cards.front: Why does a female cat heterozygous for X-linked orange and black alleles show patches of both colours rather than one colour or a blend?
cards.back: X inactivation silences one X in each cell early, and descendants keep the choice. Patches expressing the orange allele sit beside patches expressing the black allele.
cards.quote: The tortoiseshell cat makes this visible: its X-linked Orange alleles produce orange and usually black patches.

cards.front: What is a calico cat, and why can X inactivation not explain its extra patches?
cards.back: A calico is a tortoiseshell with an autosomal white-spotting allele. That allele is not on the X, so X inactivation does not explain its patches.
cards.quote: A calico is a tortoiseshell with an autosomal white-spotting allele, which adds patches that X inactivation does not explain.

cards.front: A normal XY male cat carries one X-linked orange allele. Could X inactivation make him tortoiseshell? Why does a tortoiseshell male usually need another karyotype?
cards.back: No. He has one X and one X-linked allele, hemizygous, so every cell expresses it; he shows one X-linked colour, not a patchwork. Tortoiseshell males are usually XXY, with two X chromosomes carrying different alleles.
cards.quote: Tortoiseshell and calico males are rare and usually XXY.

cards.front: Why can girls with a mutation in the X-linked gene MECP2 (Rett syndrome) differ in how their cells behave?
cards.back: X inactivation makes a girl a mosaic: her cells can differ in which MECP2 allele they express.
cards.quote: Mosaicism also matters in Rett syndrome, which mainly affects girls and involves X-linked MECP2

cards.front: How do flies balance X dosage, and what noncoding RNAs help?
cards.back: The male-specific lethal (MSL) complex coats the single male X, with roX1 and roX2, and raises its transcription toward the output of two female X chromosomes.
cards.quote: The MSL, or male-specific lethal, complex coats the single male X with help from the noncoding RNAs roX1 and roX2.

cards.front: In female flies, how does Sex-lethal prevent the male dosage compensation complex from forming?
cards.back: It blocks translation of the mRNA for MSL2, the subunit that starts complex assembly.
cards.quote: In females, Sex-lethal blocks translation of the mRNA for MSL2, the subunit that starts complex assembly.

cards.front: MSL2 is forced to be expressed in female flies. Predict what happens to the complex and to female viability, using the rule for how Sex-lethal normally acts.
cards.back: The complex gathers on their X chromosomes and lowers female viability. Sex-lethal normally blocks MSL2 translation, so forcing MSL2 bypasses that block.
cards.quote: Forcing MSL2 into females gathers the complex on their X chromosomes and lowers female viability.
cards.section: How fly and worm compensation differ

cards.front: How do XX hermaphrodite C. elegans compensate for X dosage?
cards.back: They reduce expression from each X by about half, matching the single X of XO males.
cards.quote: In the nematode C. elegans, XX hermaphrodites instead reduce expression from each X by about half, matching the single X of XO males.
cards.section: How fly and worm compensation differ

cards.front: A woman carries a mitochondrial DNA variant her husband lacks. Which of her grandchildren can carry it, through her son and through her daughter?
cards.back: Her son's children cannot, because he generally does not pass on mitochondrial DNA. Her daughter's children can, since daughters pass it on to sons and daughters.
cards.quote: sons and daughters inherited the pattern, but only daughters passed it on.

cards.front: In Baur's Pelargonium, from which parent were plastids inherited?
cards.back: From both parents. Paternal or biparental organelle transmission occurs in other species too.
cards.quote: Baur's Pelargonium showed plastid inheritance from both parents, and paternal or biparental organelle transmission occurs in other species.

cards.front: {{c1::Genomic imprinting}} means a subset of nuclear genes is expressed from only one parental allele.
cards.quote: Genomic imprinting explains the difference: a subset of nuclear genes is expressed from only one parental allele.

cards.front: Which mouse experiment showed that maternal and paternal nuclear genomes are not functionally equivalent?
cards.back: Embryos built with two maternal or two paternal genomes failed to complete development, while controls with one genome of each kind did.
cards.quote: Instead, neither uniparental group did, while the one-of-each controls did.

cards.front: In the mouse embryo experiments, why were controls operated on but left with one maternal and one paternal genome?
cards.back: They show the failure is not caused by the manipulation itself, because they were handled the same way and still developed.
cards.quote: Controls underwent the same manipulation but kept one genome of each parental kind.

cards.front: What is the chief imprinting mark, and why does it follow the parent rather than the grandparent?
cards.back: DNA methylation at imprinting control regions. It is erased in each generation's primordial germ cells and rewritten according to the animal's sex.
cards.quote: The mark therefore follows the parent, not the grandparent.

cards.front: In mouse, which parental allele of Igf2 is expressed in most tissues, and which allele of the nearby H19?
cards.back: Igf2 is expressed from the paternal allele; H19 from the maternal allele.
cards.quote: In mouse, the growth-factor gene Igf2 is expressed from the paternal allele in most tissues; nearby H19 is expressed from the maternal allele.

cards.front: A female mouse inherited a null Igf2 allele from her father and is small. She mates with a wild-type male. What size are her offspring, and why?
cards.back: All normal. A null allele passed by her is the maternal copy, which is not the expressed copy, and her offspring get a working paternal copy. The mark is rewritten by her sex, so her own paternal history does not carry on.
cards.why: Rule: the mark follows the parent, and Igf2 is expressed from the paternal allele.
cards.quote: A disrupted paternal Igf2 makes a mouse small, while the same allele inherited from the mother leaves size normal.

cards.front: In humans, which syndrome follows loss of the paternal contribution at 15q11-q13, and which follows loss of the maternal contribution?
cards.back: Paternal loss causes Prader-Willi syndrome; maternal loss causes Angelman syndrome.
cards.quote: Loss of the paternal contribution causes Prader-Willi syndrome; loss of the maternal contribution causes Angelman syndrome.

cards.front: Where is X inactivation not random?
cards.back: The paternal X is inactivated in mouse extraembryonic tissues and in marsupials. It is random in the mouse embryo proper.
cards.quote: It is random in the mouse embryo proper, but the paternal X is inactivated in mouse extraembryonic tissues and in marsupials.

cards.front: After MSL2 knockdown in male Drosophila cells, the control-to-knockdown ratio of X-linked signal averages 1.25. What fraction of control signal remains, and what is the percentage drop?
cards.back: Knockdown signal is control divided by 1.25, which is 0.80 of control, so a 20 percent drop. This is smaller than twofold.
cards.quote: MSL knockdown measured an effect smaller than twofold, so other mechanisms may contribute.
cards.section: How fly and worm compensation differ
